You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

steps.input: entry = await rlm.harness.create_memory(title="ARC periodic color pattern from sparse zero-masked grid", content="Continual-ARC task-5aa69948. Infer a repeating color sequence from nonzero cells, treating 0 as missing/background, and fill the grid with the periodic pattern. In stripe examples, each row is a uniform color; read one color per row, find the smallest period p such that all known row indices congruent mod p have the same color, then use each observed color to fill missing indices and repeat the sequence through all rows. Example task test sequence [0,0,9,1,4,6,7,6,0,0] gives p=6 pattern [7,6,9,1,4,6], hence output rows [7,6,9,1,4,6,7,6,9,1]. In a 2D diagonal-pattern example, apply the same idea to diagonal offsets (col-row): output color depends only on (col-row) mod period; the observed offsets constrain the periodic diagonal sequence. General approach: identify the repeated axis/coordinate of the pattern, infer the shortest consistent period using nonzero observations, then propagate; preserve grid dimensions. Demo examples: 25-row stripes inferred period 8, output [8,2,8,9,7,4,7,1] repeated; 28-row stripes inferred period 4, [9,3,7,7] repeated. Avoid assuming rows are always the pattern axis when input is a 2D diagonal pattern.", global_=True)
